JSON: Name: cubic_sno2_co_sensor Title: Sol–gel synthesized nanostructured cubic-phase SnO2 thin-film chemiresistive sensor for room-temperature trace carbon monoxide detection Short Hypothesis: Nanostructured cubic-phase SnO2 thin films with predominant (111) surface termination produce larger CO adsorption free energy and greater CO-induced charge transfer than tetragonal SnO2, resulting in a statistically significant increase in chemiresistive response and lower limit of detection for CO at room temperature. Related Work: Metal-oxide semiconductor (MOS) chemiresistive sensors have been widely studied for CO detection using materials such as tetragonal SnO2, ZnO, In2O3 and hybrids, often enhanced by noble-metal decoration or heterojunctions. Existing approaches typically require elevated operating temperatures (≥150–360°C) to activate gas–surface reactions, which increases power consumption and complicates deployment. Low-temperature or room-temperature solutions rely on catalytic additives, nanostructuring, or novel morphologies but still face limitations in detection limit, selectivity against common interferents (NO2, NH3, VOCs), and humidity sensitivity. Phase control of SnO2 has been less explored; reports focus on the rutile/tetragonal forms with limited ability to stabilize alternative polymorphs at ambient conditions. Key unresolved issues are (1) achieving stable, repeatable low-temperature activity without catalytic noble metals or heaters, (2) separating the effects of surface defect chemistry (oxygen vacancies) from intrinsic surface polarity/termination on adsorption selectivity, (3) reliably producing phase- and facet-controlled thin films with reproducible sensing performance, and (4) demonstrating trace-level ppb detection under variable humidity and mixed-gas backgrounds. Abstract: This project investigates a room-temperature chemiresistive sensor architecture based on nanostructured cubic-phase SnO2 thin films synthesized by a scalable sol–gel and spin-coating route. The research addresses the problem of achieving trace-level carbon monoxide (CO) detection without external heating or noble-metal catalysts. We propose to stabilize the pyrite-like cubic polymorph with dominant (111) surface termination and to exploit its surface polarity and adsorption energetics to increase CO affinity and charge-transfer response. The main contributions are (1) reproducible fabrication and structural characterization of cubic-phase SnO2 thin films, (2) systematic experimental comparison of cubic versus tetragonal SnO2 sensors under controlled gas mixtures and humidity, and (3) combined first-principles and device-level analysis linking surface termination to sensing metrics. Expected outcomes include demonstration of sub-ppb to low-ppb CO detection limits, improved selectivity against common interferents at ambient conditions, and mechanistic insight tying facet-dependent adsorption energies to chemiresistive signals, informing low-power trace-gas sensor design. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Fabricated sensor devices: at least 5 independent batches for each condition (n>=5 devices per condition). Conditions: cubic-phase SnO2 thin films (optimized sol–gel + spin coat, anneal 200°C), tetragonal-phase SnO2 thin films (control: same precursor but anneal at conditions producing tetragonal phase), cubic SnO2 with noble-metal (Pd, Au) decoration, commercial MQ-7 module, ZnO thin-film sensor, and In2O3 nanofiber sensor. CO concentration series: 1 ppb, 5 ppb, 10 ppb, 50 ppb, 100 ppb, 500 ppb, 1 ppm, 2 ppm, 5 ppm. Interferent gases: NO2 (2 ppm), NH3 (2 ppm), H2 (2 ppm), CO2 (400 ppm background probe), ethanol (2 ppm), acetone (2 ppm). Humidity levels: 15%, 30%, 40%, 50%, 60% RH. Time stability dataset: repeated 26-cycle ON/OFF (15 min ON / 15 min OFF) and long-term monitoring over 60 days and monthly up to 6 months. Baselines: tetragonal SnO2 thin film (morphology-matched), same cubic films with intentionally reduced (111) orientation, cubic films annealed at different temperatures (150°C, 250°C), commercial MQ-7, and metal-decorated SnO2. Evaluation metrics: sensor response R% = (I_gas - I_ref)/I_ref × 100, limit of detection (LOD) defined by 3σ of baseline noise, response time (t_90 rise), recovery time (t_10 fall), selectivity factor S_gas = R_CO / R_interferent, baseline noise (RMS), signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) at each concentration, drift rate (% change/day) for long-term stability, reproducibility (%RSD across devices), and adsorption/desorption activation energies estimated from Arrhenius plots. Experimental setup: gas delivery with certified CO cylinder and mass flow controllers to produce target concentrations with 80% N2 / 20% O2 carrier, total flow 500 sccm, humidity control via bubbler or humidity generator; sensor mounted on temperature-controlled stage enabling 20–100°C measurements; electrical readout via source-measure unit (e.g., Keithley 2450) in two-terminal chemiresistive mode with fixed bias voltage 0.1 V and sampling interval 1 s. Complementary DFT calculations: compute adsorption enthalpies/energies and charge transfer for CO, O2, NO2, NH3 on (111) cubic and (001) tetragonal surfaces, with/without one-to-many water molecules per surface supercell; predict preferred adsorption sites and surface vacancy formation energies. Comparison/ablation studies: (A) phase comparison: cubic vs tetragonal with matched particle size and thickness; (B) facet/orientation ablation: films with predominant (111) vs mixed orientations; (C) morphology ablation: nanoparticle size series (15–300 nm); (D) humidity ablation: same device at 15%–60% RH; (E) noble-metal decoration: with/without Pd or Au; (F) annealing temperature series to vary vacancy concentration and density. Statistical analysis: report mean ± s.d. across n>=5 devices, compute significance (t-test or ANOVA) for response differences, and determine LOD by linear fit of calibration curve and 3σ noise threshold. Data products: calibration curves, adsorption energetics table, time-series I(t) data, and device-to-device variation statistics. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: inability to reproducibly stabilize cubic-phase SnO2 across fabrication batches; uncontrolled phase mixing (cubic/tetragonal) leading to inconsistent sensing; film delamination or morphological changes during annealing or operation. Measurement biases and limits: baseline electrical noise and instrument resolution may limit claimed sub-ppb LOD; gas dilution precision at sub-ppb levels can be a source of error. Data/evaluation biases: controlled-lab gas mixtures do not capture complex real-world atmospheres (multiple interferents, particulates), limiting generalization. Humidity and surface water: strong humidity dependence may mask or reduce CO response and alter adsorption energetics; competitive adsorption by water can reduce active site availability. Cross-sensitivity: oxidizing gases (NO2, O3) and common VOCs may produce false positives or inverse response, complicating selectivity in ambient air. Scalability and manufacturability: sol–gel spin coating and phase control may be difficult to scale to large-area uniform films or CMOS-compatible processes; device-to-device variability may be high. Stability limits: long-term chemical aging, contamination, and thermal cycling may change surface chemistry and degrade performance. Computational limitations: DFT predictions may not capture finite-temperature kinetics, coverage effects at realistic humidity, or complex multi-species reaction pathways, limiting direct translation of computed adsorption energies to macroscopic sensor response.
